[h1] Lightning in a bottle [/h1]

Two of the most important elements of a good game are [b] Engaging Core Gameplay Mechanics [/b] and its [b] Replayability Value [/b] , RE4 exceeded these conditions in leagues above any other games.

During the period when the Resident Evil series was going through an identity crisis, longtime collaborator Hideki Kamiya was assigned to give resident evil a fresh new start but his vision strayed far away from the classic Resident Evil formula, ultimately Shinji Mikami (Creator of Resident Evil franchise) stepped in and made a game that revolutionised the third-person shooter genre forever. 

The combination of Tank controls with the new Over-The-Shoulder camera made for a refreshing take in the horror-action genre unlike anything that ever came before. Taking the freedom of movement away from the player is never a good move but in a horror game it works on the contrary. It adds another layer of tension and uncertainty for the player to keep in mind while trying to survive an already hostile environment. For someone who's accustomed to modern triple AAA shooters, this took some time to getting adjusted to, but with the laser-point accuracy of your shots and the super-responsive controls in accordance with your actions led to a very satisfying gun combat experience. 

The story has its usual Resident Evil charm to it - Memorable boss fights, Unique locations and Amazing Action Set-Pieces spaced out well enough to keep you engaged and also keeping the story well-paced complimented with Leon's unapologetic charisma and confidence with his one-Liners as a cherry-on-top over everything. 

Combine everything I said above together and you will have a game that will provide a unique challenge but will also the provide you the tools to overcome that said challenge, making you want to revisit everytime for some more. Truely a [b] Lightning in a Bottle [/b] experience.

[h3] FUN FACT [h3] : Resident evil 4 went through 4 iterations before settling down on the final product that we see today. The very first iteration under Hideki Kamiya was so far devoid of the Resident Evil formula that CapCom gave him the permission to turn it into his own game which eventually became the [b] "Devil May Cry" [/b]  series and the 2nd iteration was turned into its own game [b]  "Haunting Grounds" [/b] , a very underrated survival horror game.

After finishing both Resident Evil 4 Remake and Resident Evil 4 (2005), I can honestly say that this is one of the rare cases where both versions deserve to be experienced.

I started with the remake, which quickly became one of my favorite games of the year. The combat feels incredible thanks to the parry system, movement is much smoother, the horror atmosphere is stronger, and the game does an amazing job modernizing almost every aspect of the original experience. Compared to Resident Evil 2 Remake, it leans much more into action, but it never completely abandons its survival horror roots. There is always tension, especially during larger encounters, and the balance between action and horror feels almost perfect.

After that, I decided to play the original Resident Evil 4, and to be honest, it completely exceeded my expectations. I knew it was considered one of the greatest games ever made, but I wasn't expecting it to hold up this well.

What impressed me the most is how well the original game balances action, horror, exploration, and resource management. Even after all these years, it never feels boring. Every chapter introduces something new, whether it's a different enemy type, a memorable boss fight, a new environment, or some completely crazy situation that keeps the adventure fresh from beginning to end.

The pacing is fantastic in both versions. There is always something happening, and neither game wastes your time. Just when you think you've seen everything, a new enemy, mechanic, or set piece appears to keep things interesting.

The original's combat is much simpler, but it's still incredibly satisfying. Managing ammunition, choosing which weapons to upgrade, and interacting with the Merchant creates an addictive gameplay loop that remains fun throughout the entire campaign. The remake expands on these ideas with better movement, parries, stealth mechanics, and more aggressive enemies, creating a deeper combat system overall.

One thing that surprised me was how much content the original game still offers. The bosses remain memorable, the level design is excellent, and the replayability is outstanding. It's one of those games that immediately makes you want to start another playthrough. Unlockables, challenges, and weapon progression give you constant reasons to come back.

Of course, the original shows its age in some areas. The controls take time to get used to, especially after playing the remake, and some sections are stronger than others. Ashley's escort segments can occasionally slow the pace, although they were nowhere near as frustrating as I expected.

The remake also isn't perfect. While the performance was much better than what I experienced in Resident Evil 2 Remake, I still had a couple of crashes during my playthrough and occasional frame drops. Thankfully, these issues were rare and never had a major impact on the experience.

What amazed me most is how modern Resident Evil 4 still feels. After finally playing the original, it's easy to understand why so many games borrowed ideas from it. At the same time, the remake shows exactly how a classic should be modernized without losing its identity.

If I had to choose, I still think Resident Evil 4 Remake is the definitive version. The gameplay improvements, expanded mechanics, stronger horror atmosphere, and overall presentation make it my preferred way to experience the game.

However, the original absolutely deserves its legendary status. It isn't just an important game historically — it's still a genuinely fantastic game today.

Very few games manage to remain this fun, replayable, and influential more than twenty years after release. After finishing both versions, I completely understand why Resident Evil 4 is considered one of the greatest games ever made.

Resident Evil 4 (2005) is not just a game—it’s a defining moment in video game history. It represents the rare convergence of bold innovation, masterful design, and unforgettable atmosphere. At a time when the survival horror genre was beginning to feel stagnant, Capcom took a massive risk by reinventing the series with a fresh third-person perspective, dynamic combat, and faster pacing—and the result was nothing short of revolutionary.

What makes RE4 truly extraordinary is its flawless balance between action and horror. From the chilling tension of the village opening to the over-the-top boss battles and eerie environments, every moment feels meticulously crafted. The game constantly evolves, introducing new enemies, mechanics, and settings without ever feeling overwhelming. It respects the player’s intelligence, encouraging strategic thinking and rewarding precision under pressure.

The characters—especially Leon S. Kennedy—are iconic, with just the right blend of grit and camp. The dialogue is endlessly quotable, the inventory system remains one of the most satisfying in any game, and the pacing is a masterclass in how to keep players hooked from beginning to end. Even today, nearly two decades later, the controls remain tight, the atmosphere gripping, and the gameplay endlessly fun.

Resident Evil 4 didn’t just influence other games—it redefined what players expected from action and horror alike. Its fingerprints can be found across the entire gaming industry, from indie horror titles to AAA blockbusters.

In short, Resident Evil 4 (2005) is a timeless masterpiece—an experience that every gamer should have at least once. It’s not just one of the best entries in the Resident Evil series; it’s one of the greatest video games ever made.

Nine years have passed since Resident Evil 4’s initial release on the GameCube and it still holds up quite well. It’s a massively influential game that helped pioneer the third person shooter genre as well as completely changed the face of survival horror.

You’ll once again fill the shoes of Leon Kennedy as he searches for the President's missing daughter, Ashley, in a remote area of Spain. She’s being held by a mysterious cult, known as the Los Illuminados who are utilizing a mind-controlling parasite called Las Plagas in order to gain power. The village that Leon first comes across is filled with infected townsfolk aptly named Ganado or “herd” in English, who are hell-bent on stopping Leon. 

Resident Evil 4 continues the tradition of offering an eccentric and ridiculous narrative that successfully links some of the franchise's biggest characters to its events but also stands well enough on its own that newcomers are not left scratching their heads.

The controls are solid and responsive but may feel somewhat strange to those that are accustomed to modern third person shooters. Leon is unable to move and shoot at the same time and must remain stationary when aiming. The camera also obscures a lot of your surroundings, adding to the overall tension and horror.

When it comes to the gameplay and combat, the Plagas-infected enemies present a satisfying challenge. They will relentlessly pursue Leon, often trying to flank him. Removing an enemies’ head will often just allow the Plagas themselves to emerge and engage Leon directly or swing around from the host’s neck. The enemies react appropriately to each wound, dropping their weapons or stumbling rewarding your aim with purpose and control. Shield bearing cult members and blind mutants with massive claws that must be dispatched by killing the parasites on their backs also refresh the enemy roster. Several satisfying boss fights provide the cherry on top of the Resident Evil 4 gameplay experience. It also features a great inventory management and upgrade system, allowing you to customize various weapons to suit your play style.

The greater focus on action does mean that scares are less frequent than they were in previous entries. Wandering around a hedge maze with Plagas infested wolves waiting to jump out of bushes and seeking keys whilst being pursued by wheezing, seemingly unstoppable regenerators are some of Resident Evil 4's few terrifying highlights during its three acts. While the first two acts are brilliantly executed, the third act loses a bit of momentum at parts, focusing more on action opposed to horror. This handful of minor grimace worthy moments is largely lost amidst the rest of the experience which will take most players fifteen or more hours on their first playthrough.

As if the main campaign wasn't long enough, Assignment Ada offers additional content as a mini game through the third act where you collect five samples of the Las Plagas parasite. Mercenaries mode challenges players to survive and kill as many enemies as possible. It's an addictive mode that would go on to become a staple of the franchise by enticing players with a risk/reward system, stringing together kills gives players a multiplier and breaking hourglasses extends the time of the session, providing a greater opportunity to post a high score.  It’s a challenging variant on the gameplay that requires mastery of each stage to unlock further content and rewards. With these additional modes, it's really easy to get thirty hours of entertainment from Resident Evil 4. If that’s not enough, there’s also a Separate Ways campaign which acts as a mini scenario B filling in Ada’s perspective of the story with new bosses, viewpoints and a new area to complete substantially fleshing out the story.

The muted, earth tone rich Spanish village that serves as Resident Evil 4's setting is a massive departure from the dark, claustrophobic and sinister mansion from the first game and the post-apocalyptic city scape of the second and third games. When it was first released, Resident Evil 4 was one of the most impressive graphical showcases of the Playstation 2 and Gamecube. With a 1080p resolution, a frame rate of 60 FPS and some rescaled textures, Resident Evil 4 looks better than ever. It still looks its age but is still capable of impressing. The atmosphere is as rich in 2014 as it was in 2005 but it's still the same game and some low-res textures can be found.

Resident Evil 4 is a bittersweet experience, along with Half-Life 2, it helped foreshadow what was to come with new hardware as well as perfectly reinvigorating and updating a franchise that was in danger of losing its appeal as new hardware changed gamers expectations. In doing so however, Resident Evil 4 shifted the franchise's inertia toward action and with the next couple installments; Resident Evil would almost entirely forsake its horror roots. With the death of Resident Evil as a horror game, much of the survival horror genre fell into mediocrity with Dead Space being one of the few titles to successfully straddle the line between action and horror before becoming a victim of the same fate. 

Resident Evil 4 is one of the greatest games of the new millennium. It maintained enough of the elements of its predecessors to be identifiable as a Resident Evil game while otherwise reinventing the franchise. Its timeless gameplay, great art direction and mostly excellent bosses make it very playable almost a decade after its original release. If you haven't played Resident Evil 4, now is as good a time as any.

Almost twenty years after its release, RE4 remains an experience that every fan of the genre absolutely must try at least once. Despite the recent remake (which I haven't finished yet, but from what I remember, it was solid), the 2005 original maintains a unique and incredibly satisfying feel. Resident Evil 4 was released in 2005 for GameCube and was later released on other platforms. It looks like Capcom wanted to significantly improve its visuals for the second PC port as the first PC port was released in 2007. The graphics are sharper than ever and the gameplay is very good, although a few small problems exist.

This game has been enhanced for 1080p resolution at 60FPS. There is keyboard and mouse support with the ability to customize the keys. Resident Evil 4 HD comes with the Separate Ways campaign to increase replay value. The keyboard and mouse work very well together, but sometimes the laser targeting is not perfect and that can lead to problems when there are multiple enemies near you or when a large boss monster is approaching.

The plot of the game begins with the kidnapping of Ashley Graham, the daughter of the president of the United States. Leon Kennedy, the well-known protagonist of the series, has been sent to a village in Spain to rescue Ashley. What happens in the Spanish village is that there is a religious cult that has released an ancient parasite called Las Plagas on to the countryside. The religious cult does not consist of zombies like other Resident Evil games. You begin fighting ganados, a group of foes who carry pitchforks and are both males and females. Later, you will meet darker and tougher foes known as cultists, religious zealots who wear red or black robes.

As Leon progresses through the story, there will be memos explaining the plan of the cult known as the Illuminados. These memos keep you well informed of the plot and it seems to get darker and darker. The environments are appropriately creepy as Leon looks for Ashely. Resident Evil 4 retains the series’ history of creepy and dark locales. There are misty forests, decrepit houses, moldy caverns, a large castle, and military facilities. The locales display diversity so that there is no monotony. Leon is joined by other characters like Luis Sera and the Ada Wong. Luis Sera is a local citizen who is willing to help Leon. Leon engages in a long shooting with the ganados while Mr. Sera helps out in this long battle. Ada Wong is a familiar figure to Resident Evil fans and has had a long relationship with Leon. There are bits and pieces of the script that indicate past romances and rivalries. However, the plot keeps you at the edge of your seat at all times, which is the way it should be for a Resident Evil game.

The graphical enhancements of the diverse locales are what make this game feel like it is not so old. The details of Leon, his allies, and enemies are impressively sharp and well defined. The walls of the castle look extremely realistic. You can see the dust falling from the ceiling of caverns that make the caverns both realistic and creepy. The textures look amazing in high resolution, but in some cases they look a little bit archaic and out of place. However, the details of the textures are sharp enough to outweigh any archaic look you may find. Military facilities make you feel like that there is a nasty experiment going on while it also feels abandoned.

The bosses are diverse and require you to figure out their main weaknesses in order to defeat them. One issue that pops up in boss battles and in other parts of the game is the quick time events. Sometimes you have to press two buttons at once very quickly to avoid key attacks or avoid deadly traps. It can feel awkward trying to press the X + C keys or the two mouse buttons while using the WASD keys in tense circumstances. While it is appropriate to have tense circumstances in a Resident Evil game, it can get frustrating trying to press two keys at once but dying in the process because of you are not able to press the buttons in time. Another issue that comes up is the laser targeting of the firearms. There are times when the laser targeting takes time to be accurate while one or more enemies are quickly approaching you. Also, the laser can twitch in the spur of the moment, leading to more difficult encounters with the various types of enemies and possible waste of ammo. Ammo is always at a premium in the game, so twitching is a bad thing in a game like this.

All firearms can be upgraded by visiting the various merchants that stand around waiting for you. Upgrading your weapons will make your shots noticeably more powerful. You can upgrade your weapons to the max so that you can be an “exclusive” weapon that will be far more powerful than the weapon you fully upgraded. The challenge is to find the pesetas scattered throughout the locales and dropped by the enemies. You will have to quite a bit of searching for pesetas and treasures with lots of value if you want to upgrade any of your firearms to the max.

There is some randomness when it comes to shooting enemies, especially in the head. Some ganados and cultists will simply fall to their deaths with a headshot. Other enemies will show their Plagas, spider-like figures that emerge from their necks, and continue to try to attack you. You can either fire a shotgun at their Plagas or use a flash grenade to finally finish them off. There are encounters that require crowd control, so you can use different types of grenades to bring some relief to these tense encounters.

Other enemies that are interesting and horrific include garradores, colmillos, and regenerators. The garradores do not attack unless they hear your sound and are blind. Their only weakness is the Plagas shown on their backs. Colmillos are terrifying dogs that can jump on top of you by surprise. Regenerators are special monstrosities in that you can only use a sniper rifle with an infrared scope to locate and shoot their Plagas on their torso.

Resident Evil 4 is worth playing for its diverse locations, creepy atmosphere, and tense encounters. The nail biting gameplay lives up to what Resident Evil fans expect from a Resident Evil game. The high resolution graphics make the PC version the definitive version to play.

Looking back at Resident Evil 4 it's almost startling how good this game ended up. It was in development for a really long time, shifted between completely different concepts and almost ended up scrapped a few times.

Yet it pulled through, and became one of the most notable action games of the 6th generation. I say action game because that was what made Resi 4 so good. 

Resi 4 does not take place in the 'states like it's predecessors. Nor do you ever fight zombies. Instead you fight infected villagers. The dev team actually did this in a very unique way. Because of how the game employs a manual aiming system, firing at different body parts produces different reactions from enemies. Like you can stumble an enemy running at you by shooting him in the legs. This provides immense amounts of strategy to fighting enemies. Adding to that enemies will work together and use the environment against you.

The atmosphere was extraordinary, the enemies were engaging and the combat was slick and new. Resi 4 might have not aged very well in the last 10 years, but it still leaves an impact that lasts a long time.

Resident Evil 4 is the end all, be all that the genre has strived for since its inception and is a fond love letter not just to fans of action or survival-horror but to people that simply like to play games.

Frenetic action and giant boss battles aside, where Resident Evil 4 succeeds, as a survival-horror game isn't so much that it's a frightening game, though there are moments where you will be scared, but its haunting atmosphere. Resident Evil 4 will send chills through your spine as its atmosphere takes center stage against seemingly impossible odds as you go off in search of the President's daughter. 

The game has the right feel to it, it does have it's action go to the forefront as it's greatest strength but it never lets the action get in the way of the atmosphere and the mood. The two combine together to make Resident Evil 4 one of the most masterful games ever made and an example of how to do the genre justice without abandoning what makes it a survival-horror game.

You will be lost in Resident Evil 4's game world for at least twenty hours and you will be compelled to play through it again, either on harder difficulties or with all of your previous items in tow for the second go around. 

The game is truly fantastic and is well worth a purchase today for those who have never played it if only to see how it's influenced games like Dead Space and Gears of War in different ways.

Overall: Whether you're a fan of Resident Evil, the survival-horror genre, action games, adventure games, or simply good games, Resident Evil 4 has all the bases covered. [h1] STEAM REVIEW TLDR [/h1]

[b] PROS [/b]

+ Great combat and gunplay
+ Great variety of guns all of which can be upgraded.
+ Memorable boss fights
+ The environment and the ambiance that comes with it.
+ Great mix of action and horror
+ Rewards the player for exploration
+ Tons of optional content

[b] CONS [/b]

- Anything and everything that involves Ashley, 
- Plenty of QTE's which can lead to some cheap deaths.

Final Score - 9 / 10

[h1] INTRO [/h1]

Resident Evil 4 has been released countless times. Now of days with the PC rerelease the game runs at 60 FPS and is way more smooth than I am used too. The question we are asking here is how is Resident Evil 4? Is it a great Resident Evil game or was it the point where the series began to feel bland? 

[h1] STORY [/h1]

The story of Resident Evil 4 is a pretty average plot overall. You're Leon Scott Kennedy, one of the survivors of the Raccoon City incident who went from being your average cop to a US government special agent. Leon has been sent to Spain, his mission, to rescue the presidents daughter Ashley Graham who has been kidnapped. Once Leon arrives at the village he discovers something is horribly wrong with the locals. He will have to fight through crazy chainsaw wielding maniacs, villagers and etc, Some of which can mutate with the disgusting virus, Plaga. You will also have to fight giant monsters. This would not be Resident Evil without some creepy mutations and monsters.

[h1] LENGTH [/h1]

The length of the game feels just right. If you are one of those people who enjoys doing everything the game offers you. You should usually get 30+ hours out of the game, This includes replaying it plus optional extras and side stuff. A first playthrough could take anywhere around 10+ hours depending on your play style.

[h1] DIFFICULTY [/h1]

One of my first great memories for this game was finally reaching the village and having to survive against countless angry villagers, only to be greeted by a man with a chainsaw who promptly lobbed off my head and killed me quite a few times. Once they are finally defeated you are treated with the games logo. I remember yelling "That's the start? That's the tutorial?" The game set itself up to be pretty rough and tough, which overall yes it's a pretty difficult game. However I feel like the difficulty is perfect, just the right amount of frustration and happiness if that makes sense. It helps that the game plays fantastically. You will be running out of ammo, fighting hordes of angry enemies even plenty of annoying super enemies that aren't even bosses. The bosses themselves are pretty fun and fair overall.

[h1] CONTROLS [/h1]

This game has some pretty fun and tight controls. Aiming even with a controller feels nice and smooth. Quick turning is a life saver. Knifing things to get items and even knife kills are even pretty easy to do. The game was made for controls even though the PC rerelease plays great with a keyboard and mouse.

[h1] GAMEPLAY [/h1]

Resident Evil 4's gameplay is fantastic. The gunplay feels fun, shooting and killing the infested enemies feels fluid and fun. Shooting enemies in the head or knees then running up and giving them a nice roundhouse kick is great for solo enemies or even knocking down a group of enemies to get back. You will be collecting tons of treasure as you proceed through the game which you can then sell to the weapons merchant to buy plenty of guns and etc. No ammo though sadly. The only major complaint I have about the gameplay is Ashley. I'm not a fan of escort quests, even though this game for the most part becomes one big escort quest. Now I can admit that Ashley is somewhat smart and does not normally get in your way while shooting however she can die very easily with her low health early game. Sometimes while she is being carried away you can simply and accidentally kill her in one shot. However the least fun bits with Ashley come from when you are controlling her yourself for her puzzle sections, made even worst with some almost instant kill QTE's that are very fast. This game does use QTE's but overall I am fine with the use of them. The only time you are forced into a heavy QTE will be late in the game when Leon comes face to face with Krauser.

[h1] MUSIC [/h1]

Before we talk about the characters I have to ask how is the music? Overall the music is very fitting. Mostly creeping ambiance to fit the atmosphere. Some eerie music to let you know when you have been spotted. The music is more fitting for use in the game than listening to out of the game. For what it's worth i think the music is great

[h1] CHARACTERS [/h1]

Throughout the game you will meet plenty of interesting characters. Our boy Leon Scott Kennedy who we have already talked about. Ashley Gram the daughter of the president who tends to be more annoying than helpful. The mysterious man Luis Sera, the merchant, friend or foe who tends to be everywhere you are, Ada Wong the sexy agent who has a crush on Leon but is always working towards her own goals. Chief Bitores Mendez the giant brick wall in Leon's path, Krauser a man from Leon's past, Ramon Salazar the head of the castle not too far from the village itself. A tiny little man who is more dangerous than he looks and has some scary looking body guards. Osmund Saddler the leader of the cult known as the Los Illuminados and someone who is very good with parasites. I like the characters in this story quite a'bit, this includes the enemies as well from the default villagers all the way to the terrifying regenerator's. I feel like this game has the right amount of spook to it's characters.

[h1] SECRETS / UNLOCKABLES / REPLAYABILITY [/h1]

This game has quite a nice amount of unlockables and extras. Outside of the main game and it's new game + carry overs we have other game modes, We have The Mercenaries in which you are trying to survive while racking up a high score while killing as skillfully and as many as you can, which leads to you unlocking more playable characters. Separate Ways in which we play through Ada Wong's campaign. Seeing what she was doing while Leon was busy saving Ashley. She even has some unique boss fights of her own. Assignment Ada, a small game mode that has Ada running around the Island collecting Plaga samples. Unlockables for the main campaign such as the infinite rocket launcher, the overpowered Chicago Typewriter, the terrifying P.R.L. 412 and etc and of course even alternate costumes for Leon and Ashley. During the story there is also an optional shooting range that's pretty fun and challenging and has you gaining collectables. So overall this game has a ton of extras and a very high amount of replayability.

[h1] FINAL VERDICT [/h1]

I love Resident Evil 4. I have since it's original release and even with the PC Rerelease. I have played it on many different consoles and each time I have enjoyed it more and more. There are not many flaws with the game itself. I find it to have a very nice variety of action and horror, Sure it's not as scary as the previous resident evil games but it still has its moments, especially with the regenerators and iron maidens. My only real large complaint with Resident Evil 4 is honestly having to hold Ashley by her hand, escorting here everywhere. Plus the playable Ashley segments are just not fun. So overall I would give this game a [b] 9/10 [/b] I highly recommend this game to anyone that has not played it and loves action games, Even more so if you like some horror in your actions games.

There are a few armfuls of games that need no introduction, and Resident Evil 4 is definitely one of them. Despite its namesake, it's actually the 13th instalment of the famed survival-horror franchise; a whopping nine releases separate it and Nemesis. Originally released for Gamecube in 2005, this title has found itself ported to nearly every console that has released since, including the PlayStation 2, 3, and 4, Xbox 360 and One, Wii, iOS, Android, and most recently, the Nintendo Switch. While many of the later releases in the series divide fans considerably, the majority of the player base can agree on one thing; Resident Evil 4 is a masterpiece. With that said, is it still as impacting in 2020, and does this PC port stack up?

Let's cut to the chase; you've probably already played Resident Evil 4. If that's the case, and you're looking to play the game on PC, then this fairly solid port has you covered. You're able to switch from the updated HD textures to the original ones, and there's even some fine folks working on full-on brand new textures, which are available via mods. The gameplay is a smooth and buttery 60 FPS, and the overall functionality of the port is high. I will admit I did have a couple of random crashes, and there are some bug and crash reports in the forums, but it seems that these problems are few and far between. Along with nice keyboard and mouse support, Xbox 360 and Xbox One controllers work well; PS3 and PS4 controllers have a lot of problems in key areas, however, and ultimately their use should be avoided. Newer generations of gamers will more than likely find themselves struggling with the controls, which are the most aged aspect of this release. Though it's a step up from tank controls, Resident Evil 4 does feel clunky and cumbersome at times, especially in the heat of the moment. With that said, it's something that can be gotten used to, and it's by no means a deal breaker... it's simply a mechanic that isn't ageing well at all. 

If you're just getting into the virus-riddled world of Resident Evil, then this title is a good place to jump in. The game opens with a generous retelling of the main events thus far; it takes place six years after the events of Resident Evil 2, the last time (at the time of release) that we saw Leon S. Kennedy in a leading role. Having traded in his S.T.A.R.S badge for a career as a government agent, Leon has been sent on a mission to rescue the president's daughter, Ashley Graham, who has been kidnapped by a mysterious cult. After travelling to an unknown area in Spain, he discovers that entire villages have become infected with a new type of parasite known as the Las Plagas; a far cry from the zombifying G-Virus he previously dealt with. Along the way some familiar friends, foes, and new enemies make themselves known, and Leon has to not only prevent Las Plagas from becoming a worldwide epidemic, he also has a limited time to remove the parasite from both himself and Ashley.

Speaking strictly in the context of main games in the franchise, Resident Evil 4 presents a lot of firsts. It's the first to follow a more linear path in terms of puzzle solving and gameplay progression. Long gone are the item hunts from previous releases, instead being replaced with solutions that are rather easy to find. It's a welcomed change of pace for most, as the core gameplay from earlier in the series has been maintained, but in turn has been put on the backburner so that players can focus on the environments, atmosphere, and story more than worrying about backtracking for items. Though it's a hit-or-miss mechanic for everyone, this is also the first Resident Evil to sport QTEs (quick time events). Survival elements also take somewhat of a backseat, though they are present; inventory management is still a necessity, but items drops and placements are charitable, and living is made all the easier by being able to purchase ammunition, guns, and health items from an NPC.

Perhaps the biggest addition to this title is having a secondary player that you must be aware of at all times when she is present. Though she isn't a constant companion like Shiva in Resident Evil 5, nor is she a helpful sidekick like Cody/Rebecca in Resident Evil Zero, Ashley is a burdensome mechanic of a whole new nature. She cannot hold her own and must be taken care of like a little puppy, as she can get hurt and die easily, thus ending the game, and she can also get carried away by enemies... which also causes a game over. She can't even jump down a ladder by herself, and only in a few areas can you make her hide so that she is definitively safe. Let's also not forget her annoying, incessant screaming "LEEOOOON! HEEEELLLP!" when she does find herself in a dangerous situation. It's always a relief when the story leads to her being separated from Leon, as she only serves to cause undue stress on the player in a game that's already focused on survival; however less to an extent of previous entries that focus may be.

Despite Ashley arguably being the worst element of Resident Evil 4, there are many, many boons that keep players coming back to this game year after year; for dozens of playthroughs. There's an impenetrable atmosphere in this release, unlike in any other entry of the franchise that has come either before it, or after it. Everything from the gloomy, isolated setting, to the landscapes, to the thick fog and pounding rain effects, it all ends up melding perfectly into one of the most ambient masterpieces of survival horror history; second only, in my opinion, to that of the original Silent Hill. There's hardly a soundtrack to speak of, therefore forcing all of the atmospheric duty to be carried out nearly solely on visuals alone. The best modern comparison that can be made is the original Dark Souls, where there's hardly any sound at all, the world is blocky and hollow, but it boasts a massive wealth of incomparable visual ambience while also instilling a sense of dreaded loneliness.

If you're a fan of horror, especially survival horror, and you haven't yet played Resident Evil 4, there's no longer an excuse. It's a timeless classic that has earned its place in video game history, alongside greats such as Silent Hill and Eternal Darkness. It's still holding itself up firmly 15 years after its initial release, despite some of its annoying mechanics and ageing control system. If you have played Resident Evil 4 and you're looking for an excuse to pick it up on yet another platform, grabbing this port on sale is your best bet. This release does come with the extra campaigns that were present on the PlayStation 2 version; Separate Ways and Assignment Ada, along with the standard Mercenaries unlock. All of these extras are available after beating the game once.

One of the most consistently fun games I've played. It also has the most badass thing I've seen in a video game: suplexing a cultist so hard his head explodes.

At its core, Resident Evil 4 is a game about action and resource management. Your ammo matters, how and when you engage enemies matters, and what you decide to keep in your inventory matters. You will have access to powerful weapons, but with limited ammo you have to decide when the best time is to use them. The over-the-shoulder tank controls will feel awkward at first, but the inability to run-and-gun like an action hero adds to the survival horror setting in my opinion, as it forces you to pick a spot and stand your ground.

One thing that RE4 nails is its difficulty. The game always has me in a constant tug-of-war, dreading the next scenario it will throw at me. Each section of the game is unique and memorable, with different kinds of challenges to keep things fresh. It also ramps up in difficulty quite early on, letting you know that this game isn't a walk in the park. However, while it is challenging, RE4 is not cruel or sadistic; if you die, you are sent back to the beginning of the area (or sometimes a checkpoint in the middle of an area), so you never lose that much progress.

With that said, there is one issue this port has. The game logic is tied to the framerate, and since this game originally ran on 30 FPS, setting it to 60 causes unusual things to happen, as well as more aggressive enemy AI. I would recommend leaving it at 30 to avoid having to deal with any bugs. I also recommend playing the game as it was originally designed, on a controller. Mouse and keys make the game a little too easy.

In my opinion RE4 is a must play, even if you've never played a Resident Evil game. It's incredibly fun, dynamic, replayable, and a testament to excellent game design.

Alright let's get the nonsense out of the way first.
As Leon Kennedy, you have to rescue the president's daughter, kill small-time Saddler, and shoot nearly a thousand not-zombies in the face. This is one of the best games ever made.

See? Easy peasy fo' sheezy. Millions of people know that this game is totally great, and it's a waste of everyone's time for me to write a long review. Still, I feel obligated to write SOMETHING, because RE4 is that damn good.

RE4 is nearly 10 years old now, and it only seems to get better with age. It's a third-person shooter that has managed to carve out the perfect identity. It's the definition of a classic. But why is that? What is it that RE4 does so well that makes it a genre-defining masterpiece?

Let's start with something basic, sound-direction. One of the most basic ideas RE4 has is that when enemies are nearby, music plays. When the music stops, that means all of the enemies are dead. This is the moment when you can release that tension. RE4 is also one of those games where you're actively harming yourself by playing music over the in-game tunes. Your view is very limited, and all you really have to keep track of your surroundings are your ears. This isn't something you'll notice in RE5 or RE6 because 95% of the time you have a partner. In RE4 your ears are going to pick up every grunt, every foot-step, every little noise, and it's going to save your life.

Speaking of partners, I honestly think Ashley is underrated. Yeah ok "LEEEOOOOOOOOOOON" gets obnoxious, but it's to be expected. This girl is way out of her element, and protag is the only person she can trust(and vice-versa I suppose, if you don't count the merchant). There's all sorts of little moments that make her welcome company. Whenever you do something cool like shoot a hatchet out of the air, she does a little fist-pump. If there is an enemy behind you, she's going to notice. She serves as a good distraction, is quick to get behind you or duck under your gun. The most dangerous areas also tend to leave nice places for Ashley to hide. Still, I dunno...maybe I just appreciate when she's around. It's like I'm getting a psychological buff. It's easy to forget that with all the ass Leon is kicking, that the situation he and Ashley are in is well and truly screwed. Any moment where it feels like things are going right is worth holding onto.

The controls and mechanics still hold up perfectly. While having all the cool diving moves in RE6 is really nice, there's something to be said about methodically evading all sorts of stuff by walking ever so slightly to the side and/or backwards. It really gives you a feel of just how much weight goes into each encounter. Movement is just so focused and creates the right amount of context. Where you stand determines so much of the enemy's behavior.  It's like an arcade beatemup. Sure you can walk right up and punch everyone, but you're bound to take a bunch of damage in the process. The trick is to move around enough so that your foes are "herded". They're in the right position and distance for you to deal with them appropriately. Losing track of enemies is dangerous, because they could get behind you, approach your sides, and then it's back to relying on your ears as well as your eyes to restore some sort of order.

There's a lot to be said about making do with what you're given, which is where RE4 also shines. A lot of shooters have to push the "variety" angle to keep encounters interesting. There's always a new type of enemy, different victory conditions, or just some gimmick. Much of RE4 is spent in combat, and these combat situations are typically Leon in an area surrounded by enemies. Early on he has to rely on blocking doors, throwing down ladders, just to keep enemies at bay. As his arsenal improves he's expected to take fight directly to the enemy, also relying on his advanced maneuverability to stay one step ahead. When old doors close, new ones open, that's what keeps a game engaging, not doing something different at every moment. RE4 knows exactly when to create moments that are actually special, not just different. They're memorable, but unless you're replaying the game you won't have to deal with them again. Whether it's just business as usual or these special moments, the core mechanics and design of RE4 are front and center. It's astonishing just how well Capcom/Mikami gets it.

RE4 also features one of the best campaigns of any time. I'd say it's at just the right length. Some would claim that the game runs a bit too long, and that some parts could trimmed or even cut entirely. This is not something I can agree with.  Nothing really feels wasted in this game. Like okay there's a kinda dumb moment where you use a crane to drop enemies into the garbage disposal. This part of the game follows shortly after discovering the regenerators and (hopefully) finding the means to destroy them. Having a goofy little moment where you toss a few las plagas in the garbage is...kinda nice. Pacing isn't always just pushing for everything to move as quickly as possible. Even very late in the game RE4 has time to throw ideas around. Unfortunately, this probably says more about the rushed nature that game development is all too easy prey for. The end levels tend to be pushed together. The only intention is that hopefully everything doesn't fall apart. RE4 had seemingly all the time in the world to get everything right and it shows.

Back to what I said about the perfect identity. First off, no disrespect to RE5 and RE6. I really enjoy and love those games as well, but they're not RE4. What makes this game such a classic is not something that can be replicated. Even if you could somehow get prime Mikami and top-of-their-game-era Capcom together again and tasked them with doing a 1:1 sequel to RE4, you'd still end up with a lesser title. RE4 is a product of its time, it has limitations, and in a way it makes those into strengths. Sure I'd be curious to see how RE4 part 2 would play with RE6 controls, but it wouldn't be the same.  I guess conceptually it'd be an improvement, but in practice...I don't think it could work. Leon dashing around like he was in a zombie-infested Vanquish sequel? Yeah not feeling that either.

Anyway to sum it all up, play through RE4 again. Appreciate it like you never have before. We'll never see another game quite like it.

Yup, this one's a banger. One of my favourite games of all time. Better than REmake, because it's got its own identity and everything's been thought of meticulously instead of aping other current games' mechanics and bloating the game. But let's dial it back before you stop reading this. Why is this "old" game so good?

Resident Evil 4 is a classic for a good reason. This game not only kickstarted third person shooting (and inspired basically everyone of them that came after), but it's also got the pacing of a well done shooter down. The Last of Us, as bemoan as I am to mention that, and other games of Naughty Dog's ilk past 2005, owe themselves to this game, not to mention Gears of War as well (although that made it so that every third person shooter had to be a cover shooter...). If you like any third person shooter, there's a good chance you owe that to the lessons learnt from this game.

Does it lose a bit of that horror in survival horror? A little bit, definitely once you get to the island, but that's a short romp near the end that basically dials everything you've learnt up until that point to 11, so it makes sense. I would highly argue that the game still feels very much like the older games to some extent, just with a bit more action. You can't make the argument that it's going in the wrong direction, when 3 and Code: Veronica tried (and didn't succeed nearly as well due to not being able to aim freely or were restricted due to the fixed camera system) to put more action elements in the old formula. You could also probably blame Capcom for limiting REmake and 0 to the GameCube, making sure it made far less profit even if one of them was good. The formula at that point had run its course, so thinking of how to evolve Resident Evil (even if the effects of it would be more disastrous past this game) was probably the right call.

The tank controls, and not being able to move while shooting, inventory managment (tetris style management never gets old) and saving on the typewriter are some things that I can think of that are reminscent of the older style. Shinji Mikami also directed this, so it's not some other person who might not understand what the franchise is yet. Third person aiming will never feel scary, so they put a lot of emphasis on the survival rather than the horror. Unlike REmake, every hit that you get feels earnt, whether it is because Leon is dealing it, or taking it. The game has fixed rules regarding shooting areas, where shooting the head or the legs WILL trigger a melee prompt, and the melee has proper I-frames so it doesn't feel cheap when you get hit immediately after doing one in REmake. The knife is the underdog of saving ammo (and MVP of the Krauser fight), and no amount of pseudo Souls parrying will ever replace it. I never felt like the game was being too unfair outside of certain cutscenes making me get hit from enemies sneaking up on me. Dynamic difficulty exists in this game, so it can make it easier or harder depending on how well you are doing, making sure the experience is never the same, and making sure you are having a good time once you get your head around learning how Leon moves.

While some modern gamers may find this movement "limiting", it is all by design. Leon is very smooth and reflexive once you understand how he moves. He can be made even smoother with re4_tweaks, and the RE4HD Project is a must use and the definitive way of playing this game, much better than Capcom's efforts of upscaling (There is an option to use fixed camera angles during Ashley's section like it is in the Japanese version, and yes, it does become scarier). The upgrade system is rewarding and gives a great sense of progression (the Merchant is also better because he's not giving silly side quests and doesn't sound British). The puzzles are nothing to bring up comparing to the old games, but the changes to bring Resident Evil into a new direction are very good where it counts. The game is cheesy in all the right ways too, and it's not really scared of it. It's not straight camp, but Leon using humour as deflection and acting a bit like an action movie hero is probably the reason why he's a fan favourite of the franchise. Umbrella may be officially gone, but the whole franchise basically lives in that company's shadow (especially relevant for Requiem), with Leon being affected by that, and in the future too. The villains also match Leon's energy, and it's just a blast to get through, unlike the dull seriousness that modern Resident Evil likes to do so much, as if it's ashamed of its past.

The only real criticisms I have are that the additional Ada campaign doesn't feel nearly as fleshed out or as meaty in the REmake, but this game is just so good in all the right ways, a masterclass in design that should be remembered. It's definitely my favourite of the bunch, even if that may feel like sacrilege to the old RE crowd (2 is my favourite out of those ones). This is also where Mercenaries starts being fun, unlike whatever it was in 3. Wesker can't counter melees, but he's still broken as hell in this. I'll never get tired of playing this one, and I can only hope that the modern crowd can put aside their need for conformity to understand why this is an enduring legend that will live on forever.

[h1] Strong and Weak Points[/h1]
The strong point that caught my eye the most was the amount of diversity that is given to the player in their gameplay choices. From which weapons they will upgrade over others and what will they prioritize as important. There is a lot of variety in sub-types of each weapon, for example, I preferred the [b]Riot Shotgun[/b] as while not as powerful as the [b]Striker[/b], can work from a distance to keep me safe from enemies. A player that favors close-quarters and damage might instead choose the [b]Striker.[/b]

At the same time, the weapon-switching in the game was terribly tedious, there is not an option to switch weapons on the fly which means anytime you want to use another you will have to press the menu button. It stops time and allows you to react to enemies but at the same time is annoying having to press the menu button so much during later parts of the game, breaking the fantastic flow of action with monotonous pauses of selecting a weapon.

[h1] Story[/h1]
The story of [b]Resident Evil 4[/b] is for the majority of the game simple and cheesy. You play as a special agent from the United States [b] Leon Kennedy[/b] who returns after his debut in [B]Resident Evil 2,[/b] he is tasked with the mission of rescuing the president daughter that has been kidnapped by members of a mysterious cult.

Interactions between some characters can be fun and entertaining because of how cheesy they are, which is something that I enjoyed a lot but at the same time, there was never a deeper plot and it lacked exposition in a meaningful way. It is like watching an action movie only that there is a lot of loose ends and it there could have been room for more material in it. 

[h1]X Notes[/h1]
Game crashes sometimes, particularly when aiming and it runs pretty well on a GTX 1060. Elements during it can be confusing because the game fails to communicate with the player, and you can have situations such as fending off a wave of enemies only to find out the main idea was to escape or activate a trap somewhere else. This waste those resources and make for missed opportunities, smart communication between the game and the player always helps.

[h1] What makes it Special[/h1]
What makes [b]Resident Evil 4[/b] special to me is that is a game that has is moments, from the tension I feel all the time when the music is playing if enemies are near, to the silent corners making me wonder if there is something monstrous in the next hallway. It is a very atmospheric game and I appreciate that. I had some good laughs with the dialogue and the few jump-scares got me pretty good because even when I was expecting some, the execution of them caught me off guard. 

I also love a lot that the game has a lot of bosses in it, I would imagine that they were running out of it at points during my run but they just kept coming and their designs range from interesting to downright creepy. They each have their own strength and weakness, making their challenge to be more enjoyable! From digging underground to shooting doors to escape and even more, each boss brought something new. 

[h1] Finally…[/h1]
[B]Resident Evil 4[/b] is a classic that is well-known to a lot of players and while this port might not be perfect, the soul of the game is intact and is worth delving into. A game that sought to re-invent the franchise and that introduces a lot of content for players to enjoy, I easily recommend this to [b]Resident Evil[/b] fans and those that want to play an amazing third-person shooter.

On February 3rd 2026 Capcom released an update to RE4 Remake that removed Denuvo, a DRM which requires a costant internet connection, and replaced it with the Enigma Protector. This DRM is supposed to prevent "cheating" (any kind of modding of the game) and it's russian developed.
Tested by the Youtube channel Digital Foundry in the video "Resident Evil 4 PC: Is New DRM Impacting Game Performance?" has been found that the Enigma Protector DRM causes an average of -10% in framerate drops, with dips of -40% in certain scenarios, way more than the original Denuvo DRM.

This is not the first time that Capcom decided to put Enigma in some of their older games: RE Revelations suffered major backlash from customers because of the major dip in perfomance, so much so they had to remove Enigma from the game for good and recently they released the original Dino Crisis series on Steam, a quick scouring of the forum will reveal a lot of customers unhappy with the perfomance of said games. Why a 25 years old single player game that should run flawlessly on a phone had to be "protected" against "cheating" is everyone's guess, especially when you realise that a GOG version of both games was already available, without the Enigma Protector and without issues.

Here's my grievances with it:

-Retroactively degrading perfomances of a game or a product is an unethical and fundamentally anti-consumer practice that should be illegal. Imagine your car having less hp out of nowhere because the car company decided to update the software that way

-Capcom degraded the game for no reasons at all, Enigma Protector doesn't prevent cheats or mods in any capable way and it's openly mocked by the mod communities

-All Capcom's game that have been "protected" by Enigma suffered of significant perfomance loss and the DRM can be easily removed by the cracking scene. The customer is therefore presented with this funny scenario: would you rather download the game for free or pay money for a degraded version that runs worst than the pirated copy?

-There's a very likely possibility that in future all Capcom's games will eventually incorporate the Enigma DRM years after launch, the system that you used to play them could eventually not being capable of the same perfomance as before, forcing some to spend money on very costly upgrades (due to the AI craze)

-The DRM is russian developed, profits from the company are most likely to be used in the ongoing russian invasion of Ukraine. This is not only unethical per-se but raises security questions for all the countries where the governments are actively funding the ukranian defense: Russia is well known to use cyber warfare against its enemies, I personally don't want anything russian developed in my system

-Enigma Protector devs in the past have behaved very unprofessionally, mocking and insulting whoever questioned the validity of their practices and their work, raising more than one red flag on the true purpose of their work and their true intent

I don't know who and why at Capcom signed a contract for this to happen but they clearly got scammed and it's time for them cope with it. I will leave a negative review on all my Capcom products and maybe I will revert them if they abandon Enigma altogether. Just maybe though, I'm kind of fed up on AAA publishers malpractices.
